subject: Polity
topic: Union Executive — Vice President and PM

concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of PM's Appointment: Article 75 vs. Convention
key_dimensions: Article 75(1) states PM is appointed by the President — no explicit mention of 'leader of majority'
Constitutional silence vs. binding convention: President must appoint leader of majority party/coalition
Discretionary power of President in hung parliament scenarios (Sarkaria Commission recommendations)
Comparison with UK Westminster model from which the convention is borrowed

concepts.name: Eligibility Conditions for Prime Minister
key_dimensions: Must be a citizen of India and member of either House of Parliament (Article 75 read with Article 84)
UPSC trap: PM need NOT be a member at the time of appointment — can be appointed and must acquire membership within 6 months
PM can be from either Lok Sabha OR Rajya Sabha — no constitutional bar (e.g., H.D. Deve Gowda, Manmohan Singh were RS members)
Age qualification: minimum 25 years (if LS) or 30 years (if RS) — often confused by aspirants

concepts.name: PM's Tenure and Security of Office
key_dimensions: Article 75(2): PM holds office during the pleasure of the President — formal constitutional position
Real protection: PM can be removed only if they lose the confidence of Lok Sabha (Article 75(3))
Tension between Articles 75(2) and 75(3): 'pleasure doctrine' vs. 'collective responsibility' — which overrides?
No fixed tenure unlike the President (5 years) — serves as long as LS confidence is maintained

concepts.name: Collective Responsibility of Council of Ministers (CoM) and PM's Role
key_dimensions: Article 75(3): Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha — NOT Rajya Sabha
PM as the linchpin: resignation of PM dissolves entire CoM (Article 74 read with 75)
Individual ministerial responsibility vs. collective responsibility — distinction and interplay
UPSC trap: CoM is responsible to LS, but PM can be from RS — implications for accountability

concepts.name: PM's Power of Portfolio Allocation and Reshuffling
key_dimensions: Constitutional source: Article 77(3) — President makes rules for allocation of business of Government on PM's advice
Convention: President allocates portfolios on PM's recommendation — President cannot act independently
PM's power to reshuffle, drop, or reassign ministers — political vs. constitutional dimensions
Limits: Constitutionally no bar, but coalition politics, Supreme Court observations (Nabam Rebia case) create practical constraints

concepts.name: PM as Head of Council of Ministers: Primus Inter Pares vs. Dominant Executive
key_dimensions: Constitutional position: 'first among equals' — all ministers are equal members of CoM
Real position: PM controls agenda, composition, and dissolution of CoM — making them dominant
B.R. Ambedkar's vision vs. actual evolution of office under strong PMs (Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Modi)
42nd Amendment (1976) made PM's advice binding on President — reinforced PM's supremacy

concepts.name: PM's Role as Communication Channel Between President and CoM
key_dimensions: Article 78: Duties of PM — communicate to President all decisions of CoM, information on administration, proposed legislation
Article 78(b): PM must furnish information the President 'calls for' — mandatory, not discretionary
Article 78(c): If President requires, PM must submit for CoM consideration decisions taken by individual ministers
UPSC trap: Article 78 is about PM's duties TO the President, not the other way — often confused with President's powers

concepts.name: PM's Advice and Presidential Discretion: Binding Nature Post-44th Amendment
key_dimensions: Original Constitution: Article 74 — CoM to 'aid and advise' President; President could return advice ONCE
44th Amendment (1978): Added proviso that President shall act in accordance with advice after reconsideration
42nd Amendment (1976): First made advice binding — 44th Amendment retained binding nature but added reconsideration clause
UPSC trap: President can return advice ONCE but MUST accept reconsidered advice — not truly discretionary

concepts.name: PM's Role in Dissolution of Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: President dissolves LS on PM's advice under Article 85(2)(b) — President's discretion is constitutionally debated
Key controversy: Can President refuse PM's advice to dissolve LS? — Sarkaria Commission, Constituent Assembly debates
Minority government scenario: Can a PM who has lost majority advice dissolution? — SR Bommai case implications
Distinction: Prorogation (Article 85(2)(a)) vs. Dissolution (85(2)(b)) — PM advises both, different consequences

concepts.name: PM's Powers of Appointment: Constitutional and Statutory Offices
key_dimensions: PM advises appointment of: Governors, CAG, Attorney General, Election Commissioners, UPSC Chairman, ambassadors
Cabinet Committee on Appointments (ACC): PM chairs — actual decision-making body for senior bureaucracy
UPSC trap: Appointment of CJI — by President on PM's advice? No — by President in consultation with judiciary (collegium), not PM
Distinction between appointments where PM's advice is decisive vs. where consultation with others is mandatory

concepts.name: PM as Chairman of Key Constitutional and Statutory Bodies
key_dimensions: PM chairs: Cabinet, Cabinet Committees (including CCEA, CCS), NDC, NDA, Inter-State Council (Article 263)
NITI Aayog: PM is ex-officio Chairperson — non-constitutional body replacing Planning Commission
UPSC trap: PM is NOT the chair of the National Human Rights Commission, Election Commission, or Finance Commission
PM's role in Space Commission, Atomic Energy Commission — executive orders, not constitutional mandates

concepts.name: Emergency Powers and PM's Role: Articles 352, 356, 360
key_dimensions: Article 352 (National Emergency): President proclaims on written advice of CoM (Cabinet) — PM's role is decisive as CoM head
44th Amendment requirement: Written advice from Cabinet (not just CoM) before President can proclaim emergency
Article 356 (President's Rule): Invoked on PM's/CoM's recommendation — Governor's report to President goes through Home Ministry under PM
UPSC trap: Under Article 352, advice must be from CABINET (senior ministers) not entire CoM — a specific 44th Amendment safeguard

concepts.name: PM's Accountability: Parliamentary Mechanisms vs. Constitutional Provisions
key_dimensions: PM accountable to LS through: Question Hour, No-confidence motion, Adjournment motion, Censure motion
No-confidence motion: Only in LS — if passed, entire CoM must resign (Article 75(3))
UPSC trap: There is NO constitutional provision for a 'confidence motion' — it is a parliamentary convention; 'no-confidence' alone is in Rules of Procedure
Anti-defection law (10th Schedule): Does NOT apply to voting on no-confidence motion — whip can compel voting

concepts.name: Acting Prime Minister and PM's Temporary Absence
key_dimensions: No explicit constitutional provision for 'Acting PM' — unlike Vice President acting as President
Convention: Senior-most Cabinet minister (often designated Deputy PM or Senior Minister) acts as PM
UPSC trap: There is no constitutional office of 'Deputy Prime Minister' — it is a political arrangement only
Comparison: Article 65 explicitly provides for VP acting as President — no equivalent article for PM's temporary vacancy

concepts.name: PM's Role in Foreign Policy and Treaty-Making Powers
key_dimensions: Article 253: Parliament has power to legislate on treaties — but negotiation/signing is executive function of PM/Cabinet
No constitutional requirement for Parliamentary approval before treaty signing — only legislation implementing it needs Parliament
UPSC trap: India joining international organizations or treaties does NOT automatically require Parliamentary ratification (unlike USA)
PM's role in 'Track I diplomacy' vs. constitutional framework — largely convention-based, not codified

concepts.name: PM's Oath of Office: Content, Administration, and Constitutional Significance
key_dimensions: Article 75(4): PM takes oath of office and secrecy before the President — Third Schedule of Constitution prescribes format
Oath contains: Allegiance to Constitution, uphold sovereignty/integrity, faithful discharge of duties, act without fear/favour
UPSC trap: PM takes TWO oaths — oath of office AND oath of secrecy (unlike President who takes one combined oath)
Oath administered by PRESIDENT — not CJI (CJI administers President's oath) — common confusion in exams

concepts.name: Checks on PM's Powers: Constitutional Limitations and Judicial Review
key_dimensions: Fundamental Rights (Part III): PM/government actions subject to judicial review — cannot violate FR
SR Bommai Case (1994): Imposed judicial check on misuse of Article 356 — indirectly limits PM's power to destabilize states
Anti-defection, RTI, CAG audit: Statutory checks on PM's authority
UPSC trap: PM's advice to President is NOT absolutely immune from judicial review — court can examine if advice was based on extraneous considerations (debated but not settled)

concepts.name: Evolution of PM's Office: Constitutional Amendments Affecting Powers
key_dimensions: 42nd Amendment (1976): Made presidential action on CoM advice mandatory; added 'socialist, secular' to Preamble — strengthened PM
44th Amendment (1978): Restored some Presidential discretion (reconsideration of advice); restored property rights amendments
91st Amendment (2003): Council of Ministers size capped at 15% of LS strength — limits PM's patronage power
UPSC trap: 91st Amendment cap applies to CoM of Union AND states — often asked whether it is uniform; also applies to coalition compulsions

concepts.name: PM's Office (PMO) vs. Cabinet Secretariat: Institutional Distinction
key_dimensions: PMO: Not a constitutional body — created by executive order; headed by Principal Secretary to PM
Cabinet Secretariat: Headed by Cabinet Secretary (senior-most IAS officer) — coordinates CoM functioning under Article 77(3)
UPSC trap: Cabinet Secretary is NOT a political appointee — is a civil servant; PMO has political appointees (OSD, advisors)
Overlap and tension: Both serve PM/Cabinet but PMO has expanded to overshadow Cabinet Secretariat in recent decades

concepts.name: PM During Caretaker Status: Constitutional and Conventional Constraints
key_dimensions: After dissolution of LS or loss of no-confidence vote, PM continues as 'caretaker' till new PM is appointed
Constitutional basis: Article 74 — President must always have a CoM; hence caretaker PM is constitutionally necessary
Conventional restraints on caretaker PM: Should not take major policy decisions, fresh financial commitments, make key appointments
UPSC trap: These restraints are CONVENTIONAL, not constitutional — caretaker PM retains full legal powers; no constitutional bar on their actions
